name: Petrichor-Deeps
description: Petrichor-Deeps is an ocean with almost no land to its name—a single world-sea of deep violet water stretching from pole to pole, broken only by volcanic island arcs rising along the equatorial rifts. A single storm system, older than any record, circles the entire planet and is visible from orbit as a pale spiral scar. Where sunlight strikes the shallows, the water glows faintly green at the crests of every wave.

The air smells of rain and salt and something sweeter underneath, like crushed stems. Nights are loud here: the sea itself gives off a low, continuous shimmer, and swimmers report the glow brightening around their limbs as trillions of microbes respond to disturbance. Dawn brings steam-fogs that roll across the lagoons in slow white banks, and the whole world feels like it is breathing.

The microbial mats of Petrichor-Deeps are its only native life, yet they have engineered an entire planet—oxygenating the atmosphere, seeding the clouds, painting the seafloor rifts in luminous colonies the size of continents. Xenobiologists argue about how long such a biosphere takes to build; the leading answer, four billion years, sits uneasily beside evidence that the ocean's chemistry was 'seeded' from outside at some point in the deep past.

The Halcyon Survey maintains a stilt-legged research outpost on the largest equatorial island, harvesting microbial compounds that have already yielded two revolutionary medicines. But the storm—locally called the Old Swirl—has begun to tighten, and the rift valleys beneath the glowing mats have started venting gas that kills the bacteria on contact. Something under the seafloor has changed, and the Survey wants to know what before it reaches the surface.
